has not had human revision or external review.  It is the platform
paper: it covers the composition layer above the kernel — hosts,
plugins, rules, kits, options, and the engines that bind them — and
cites the kernel paper [@handl2026kernel] for the arrow calculus,
the `Term`/`Value` model, the `Language` schema, and the graded

implementation names the crate, module, or file that carries it;
the repository is `handl-lang/host`, and the API excerpts are drawn
from `crates/platform/src/`.

# Introduction

Two couplings make a language toolchain expensive to grow.  The first
is *language-to-tool*: each new construct is a new obligation on the
parser, the evaluator, the typechecker, the formatter, the linter, and
every analysis, so tools disagree in proportion to the language's
surface.  The kernel paper [@handl2026kernel] attacks that coupling by
making a language pure data — a `Language` value assembled from
fragments — and making every engine generic over it.

The second coupling is *tool-to-host*, and it is this paper's subject.
Even with a data-driven language, someone must decide which languages,
engines, operations, library functions, and options a given running
tool contains.  The usual answers — a hardcoded main, a bespoke plugin
interface per subsystem, an extension registry per tool — reproduce
the original problem one level up: every subsystem invents its own
composition rules, and two tools that should share components cannot.

The handl platform's answer is to refuse the distinction.  Everything
a host loads is a `Plugin`; the only real sub-distinction is whether a
plugin also implements `RuleAcceptor` — whether it accepts
contributions.  A library is a plugin that registers more plugins.  A
target is a plugin that contributes rules for a compilation-shaped
operation.  An operation is a plugin that accepts rules and answers a
capability.  An option set is a plugin that accepts schemas.  A
formatter, an evaluator, a garbage collector, and a module of host
functions are the same kind of thing viewed from the composer.

Concretely, the paper describes:

- @sec-host — the composable host: `Plugin`, `CapabilityId`,
  `CapabilityRequest`/`CapabilityResponse`, `PluginRegistry`, and
  `DefaultHost`'s `load`/`run` lifecycle;
- @sec-rules — rules as typed contributions: `Contribution`,
  `RuleAcceptor`, `Operation`, `Behavior`, and the
  `contribute::<P>` channel with deferred delivery;
- @sec-operations — operations as acceptor plugins, including the
  `Eval` operation whose context *is* a serializable continuation;
- @sec-compose — manifests and composition resolution:
  `PluginManifest`, `resolve`, and the `ResolvedComposition`;
- @sec-kits — kits and configuration: `Kit`/`KitManifest`,
  `HostConfig`/`.handl.toml`, and `OptionsPlugin`/`ResolvedOptions`;
- @sec-engines — the engines as data-driven machinery in the
  `engine-*` family, bound by name through `handl-runtime`'s
  `EngineRegistry`;
- @sec-tensor — `host-tensor`, a worked example of a capability
  surface composed entirely through the plugin model;
- @sec-principles — the design principles the model operationalises;
- @sec-status — the public workspace map and the honest boundaries.

The design claim is narrow: *one plugin model plus a
capability-indexed registry plus a fixed-point contribution pass is
sufficient to assemble every tool in a language toolchain from the
same pieces.*  The evidence is the repository itself: the composer is
roughly two hundred lines of `host.rs`, the resolver is data over
manifests, and nothing in `handl-platform` knows what a "language" is.

# The layer below {#sec-kernel}

The platform sits on the kernel, and this section is deliberately
short — the kernel paper owns the calculus narrative
[@handl2026kernel].  What this layer needs to know:

- Everything that executes is a `Term` in a closed six-combinator
  arrow calculus (`arr`, `>>>`, `first`, `choice`, `loop`, `app`),
  extended with `Op`/`Handle` for graded algebraic effects; arrow
  values are self-contained serializable data, not closures
  [@hughes2000arrows; @lindley2010arrow; @sanada2024arrows;
  @handl2026kernel].
- A language is a `Language` value — a set of fragment tables
  (`tokens`, `lexer_rules`, `grammar`, `ast`, `eval`, `types`,
  `transforms`, `options`, `laws`, `rewrites`, …) merged with
  override/collision semantics, not code compiled into an engine.
- Engines are *models* of that data: the staged contract is
  `lex(lang, src)`, `parse(lang, toks)`, `eval(lang, ast)`, and
  `run = eval ∘ parse ∘ lex`; dispatch on node kind goes through
  `lang.eval`/`lang.grammar`/`lang.ast` child roles, never a
  hardcoded `match`.

The platform's job is everything the kernel refuses to do: decide
*which* `Language` is loaded, *which* engines interpret it, *which*
operations exist, *which* host functions programs may call, and *what
configuration* applies.  Where the kernel says "a model interprets
terms", the platform says "a host loads the plugins that provide the
models".  The kernel's `ArrSource::Foreign` and
`ModuleLookup`/`Function` seam is exactly where the platform's world
of host functions plugs in (@sec-tensor).

# The composable host {#sec-host}

## One trait

`handl-platform` (`crates/platform`) defines the universal, object-safe
extension point.  The real signature — verified against
`crates/platform/src/plugin.rs` — is:

```rust
pub trait Plugin: Send + Sync + Any {
    fn id(&self) -> &str { self.name() }
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
    fn version(&self) -> &str { "0.0.0" }
    fn capabilities(&self) -> &[CapabilityId];
    fn requires(&self) -> &[CapabilityId] { &[] }
    fn optional(&self) -> &[CapabilityId] { &[] }
    fn metadata(&self, capability: &CapabilityId) -> Option<CapabilityMetadata>;
    fn manifest(&self) -> Option<&PluginManifest> { None }

    fn contribute(&self, _ctx: &mut ContributionContext)
        -> Result<(), PlatformError> { Ok(()) }

    fn run(&self, request: &CapabilityRequest, ctx: &mut PluginContext)
        -> Result<CapabilityResponse, PlatformError>;

    fn module_lookup(&self) -> Option<Rc<dyn ModuleLookup>> { None }
}
```

Three phases are visible in the signature.  **Discovery** is
declarative: `id`/`name`/`version`, the `capabilities` a plugin
provides, the `requires`/`optional` capability dependencies it
declares, and an optional `manifest` for plugins that participate in
composition resolution (@sec-compose).  **Composition** is
`contribute`: during `load`, each plugin gets a mutable
`ContributionContext` through which it can register more plugins and
deliver typed rules to acceptors (@sec-rules).  **Execution** is
`run`: a capability request plus a `PluginContext` that hands the
plugin mutable access back to both registries.

The capability wire format is deliberately thin:

```rust
pub struct CapabilityRequest {
    pub capability: CapabilityId,
    pub payload: serde_json::Value,
}
pub struct CapabilityResponse(pub serde_json::Value);
```

`CapabilityId` is a newtype string; `CapabilityMetadata` is `Value`.
A capability request is serializable end to end — which is what lets
the same dispatch serve in-process closures, manifest-loaded plugins,
and out-of-process providers (@sec-kits).

## The registry and the host

`PluginRegistry` is a vector of `Arc<dyn Plugin>` plus a
`HashMap<CapabilityId, usize>` index (`plugin.rs`).  `register`
indexes each declared capability; `resolve(&cap)` returns the provider;
`run` resolves and invokes; `get_plugin_mut::<P>`/`get_plugin::<P>`
downcast to concrete types — the channel `contribute::<P>` is built
on.  Two registries is all the state a host carries:

```rust
pub struct DefaultHost {
    plugins: PluginRegistry,
    kits: KitRegistry,
}
```

`DefaultHost` is an *empty composer*.  Its lifecycle is two calls:

- **`load(&mut self) -> Result<(), PlatformError>`** — the
  contribution pass.  `host.rs` iterates the registry, calling each
  plugin's `contribute` exactly once in registration order; because
  plugins registered during the pass extend `plugins.len()`, the loop
  bound grows until no new plugins appear — a fixed point over
  registration order.  After each `contribute`, deferred rule
  contributions are retried (@sec-deferred); after the pass, pending
  exclusions are applied and any still-unresolved acceptor names fail
  with `MissingRuleAcceptor`.
- **`run(&mut self, &CapabilityRequest) -> Result<CapabilityResponse,
  PlatformError>`** — capability dispatch: resolve the capability to
  its provider, invoke `plugin.run` with a `PluginContext` borrowing
  both registries.  An unprovided capability is
  `PlatformError::UnknownCapability`, not a panic.

`resolve_composition` is the read-side validation: it builds manifests
from the live registry (`Plugin::manifest`, synthesised when absent)
and runs the manifest resolver (@sec-compose) against them, so a host
can ask "is this composition coherent?" without a kit.

```rust
let mut host = DefaultHost::new();
host.register_plugin(GreetPlugin::new());   // provides "greet"
host.load()?;
let resp = host.run(&CapabilityRequest {
    capability: "greet".into(),
    payload: json!({"name": "alice"}),
})?;
```

The example is the published tutorial's
(`docs/site/tutorials/build-a-host.md`, and `write-a-plugin.md` adds
the contribution path); it is included because it is the whole idea —
the host started empty and ended as a tool that can `greet`.  Nothing
distinguishes this from a language server except the plugins loaded.

Two stock plugin forms cover the common providers.  `InProcessPlugin`
wraps a closure
`Fn(&CapabilityRequest, &mut PluginContext) -> Result<CapabilityResponse, PlatformError>`
as a plugin.  `ProcessPlugin` represents an out-of-process provider:
with no run function it reserves the capability id and answers
`NotImplemented`; `with_run_fn` makes it live.

`CallableLookup` (a two-getter trait over the registries) and
`Vm<CallableLookup, Env>` (`vm.rs`) decouple the minimal VM wrapper
from `DefaultHost` itself — the "VM" is a host plus an environment,
generic over both.

# Rules as typed contributions {#sec-rules}

The contribution vocabulary is four traits
(`crates/platform/src/plugin_model.rs`):

```rust
pub trait Contribution: Send + Sync + 'static {
    fn id(&self) -> &str;
}

pub trait RuleAcceptor: Plugin {
    type Rule: Contribution;
    fn accept(&mut self, rule: Self::Rule) -> Result<(), PlatformError>;
}

pub trait Operation: Send + Sync + 'static {
    type Request;
}

pub trait Behavior<Op: Operation>: Send + Sync + 'static {
    fn kind(&self) -> &str;
    fn apply(&self, op: &mut Op::Request) -> Result<(), PlatformError>;
}
```

An `Operation` is a marker type whose associated `Request` is the
mutable record a rule acts on.  A `Behavior<Op>` handles one
`AstNode.kind` — and the AST itself is not an enum but a single open
node type:

```rust
pub struct AstNode {
    pub kind: String,      // keyed to registered Behaviors
    pub span: Option<Span>,
    pub payload: serde_json::Value,
}
```

So "a formatter rule for `comment` nodes" is `impl Behavior<Format>`
with `kind() == "comment"`, and "a new language construct" is a set of
behaviors — one per relevant operation — contributed for a kind the
platform has never heard of.  This is the platform-level counterpart of
the kernel's dispatch-on-data rule: the platform does not know the
operations' node vocabularies either.

## `contribute::<P>`: typed delivery

`ContributionContext` is what a plugin sees during `load`.  Its key
method:

```rust
pub fn contribute<P: RuleAcceptor>(&mut self, rule: P::Rule)
    -> Result<(), PlatformError>
```

The type parameter `P` pins the acceptor's `Rule` associated type at
compile time: a `Format` behavior cannot be contributed to a linter —
the delivery is type-safe, while the *addressing* is dynamic (by
concrete type, resolved through `get_plugin_mut::<P>`).  The context
also offers `register_plugin`, `resolve`/`run` for invoking
capabilities of already-loaded plugins during composition,
`has_plugin_id`, `exclude_plugin` (deferred removal), and
`contribute_exec_control` for the evaluator's hook channel
(@sec-operations).

## Deferred contribution {#sec-deferred}

`contribute::<P>` does not require `P` to be loaded first.  If the
acceptor is absent, the rule is boxed into a `PendingRule` — a closure
over the rule slot that retries `accept` against the registry — and
queued.  `DefaultHost::load` calls `flush_pending_rules` after every
`contribute`, so a rule is applied as soon as its acceptor appears;
any acceptor names still unresolved at the end fail the load with
`MissingRuleAcceptor`.  Loading order is therefore a convenience, not
a constraint: a kit may register a rule plugin before the operation it
targets, and a library plugin's `contribute` may register the acceptor
itself.

# Operations as acceptor plugins {#sec-operations}

The platform ships the generic operation contracts in the same crate.
Each follows one shape — a marker `Operation`, a `Request` record
carrying the `AstNode` plus `ResolvedOptions`, a `Behavior<Op>` alias,
and a `Basic*` `RuleAcceptor` plugin that holds `rules` keyed by kind:

|| Operation | Request fields | `Basic*` acceptor | Capability |
||---|---|---|---|
|| `Format` | `ast`, `output`, `options` | `BasicFormatter` | `fmt` |
|| `Lint` | `ast`, `diagnostics`, `options` | `BasicLinter` | `lint` |
|| `Compile` | `ast`, `compiled`, `options` | `BasicCompiler` | `compile` |
|| `Build` | `ast`, `built`, `options` | `BasicBuilder` | `build` |
|| `Eval` | `ast`, `ctx`, `options`, `result` | `BasicEvaluator` | `eval` |

: The built-in operation acceptors (`format.rs`, `lint.rs`,
`compile.rs`, `build.rs`, `eval.rs`). {#tbl-operations}

Dispatch is uniform: `run` lifts the request payload into an `AstNode`
whose `kind` selects which registered rules `apply`.  These `Basic*`
acceptors are the *contribution seam* — the place per-kind rules land
— not the canonical toolchain engines; the actual pipelines are the
data-driven `engine-*` layer bound over `Language` (@sec-engines).
The two exist for different reasons and the crate documents the seam
honestly: acceptors compose Rust behavior per node kind; engines
interpret `Language` data wholesale.

## Eval is the rich operation

`Eval` is where the uniform pattern needs more, and `eval.rs` shows
why the model still holds.  `EvalRequest` carries an `EvalContext`:
a stack of variable scopes, `EvalLimits` (`max_depth`, `max_calls`), a
call counter, and — critically — an `EvaluatorCallback` recursion
handle so a rule evaluates children via `req.ctx.eval(&child)`.

Two consequences matter:

- **The context is the continuation.**  `EvalError::Yield { context }`
  suspends evaluation; the context serializes (runtime handles are
  `#[serde(skip)]`), and `BasicEvaluator::resume` re-attaches the
  evaluator and module lookup and continues.  A `Host` can catch
  `PlatformError::Yield`, persist the context, and resume later — the
  resumable-computation story of the kernel's `Op`/`Handle` carried
  into the operation layer.
- **Cross-cutting execution is a two-hook seam, not middleware.**
  `ExecControl` contributes `before_eval`/`after_eval` hooks invoked
  around every dispatch; `before_eval` may return
  `ControlFlow::Skip(value)` to short-circuit with a cached result.
  Limits, tracing, caching, and sandboxing are contributed rules —
  delivered through `contribute_exec_control` with the same deferred
  machinery — rather than evaluator internals.

The module boundary is the last piece of the eval story.
`Module`/`Function`/`ModuleLookup` define qualified host functions
(`math.add`), `ModuleRegistry` (in `plugin-module`) resolves them, and
any plugin may expose a registry through `Plugin::module_lookup`.  The
evaluator wires the first registry it finds into `EvalContext`, so
`call_function("math.add", …)` works for every contributed rule
without the evaluator knowing any module names.  This is "the host
provides the world" (@sec-principles) made concrete: which functions
exist, which namespaces are available, and what effects are permitted
are all load-time composition facts.

# Manifests and composition resolution {#sec-compose}

Discovery in the small is `capabilities()`/`requires()`/`optional()`
on the trait.  Discovery in the large — before anything is registered
— is `PluginManifest` (`manifest.rs`), pure serializable data:

|| Field | Type | Meaning |
||---|---|---|
|| `id`, `version` | `String` | identity; version defaults `"0.0.0"` |
|| `provides` | `Vec<CapabilityId>` | capabilities offered |
|| `requires` / `optional` | `Vec<Dependency>` | hard / soft deps — `Dependency::Capability{capability, version}` or `Dependency::Plugin{id, version}` |
|| `extends` | `Vec<ExtendsDeclaration>` | plugin → extendee (+ optional `extension_point`) |
|| `conflicts` | `Vec<ConflictDeclaration>` | plugin- or capability-level exclusions, with `reason` |
|| `replaces` | `Vec<String>` | plugin ids superseded |
|| `targets` | `Vec<TargetCompatibility>` | per-target `TargetSupportLevel`: `Supported`/`Exact`/`Lossless`/`Lossy`/`Checked`/`Emulated`/`Unsupported` |
|| `exclusive` | `Vec<CapabilityId>` | capabilities that may not have multiple providers |
|| `metadata` | `Value` | opaque loader data (e.g. a native library `path`) |
|| `ast_kinds` | `Vec<AstKindDeclaration>` | `Produces`/`Consumes` claims over node kinds |

: The `PluginManifest` schema. {#tbl-manifest}

`resolve(manifests, selectors, target)` (`resolve.rs`) is the
composition checker — a deterministic pass over the manifest data,
not a SAT solver:

1. Reject two manifests with the same id at different versions.
2. Build the provider map: a `CapabilitySelector` pins a provider
   (validated — the pin must actually provide the capability); a
   capability with one provider maps to it; multiple providers are an
   error only if the capability is `exclusive`, otherwise the highest
   semver wins.
3. Check every `requires`: capability deps resolve through the
   provider map, plugin deps by id, both with `VersionReq` checking —
   failures are `MissingCapability`/`MissingPlugin`/`VersionMismatch`.
   Unresolved `optional` deps are *recorded* in `missing_optional`,
   not failed.
4. Check `conflicts`; build `extension_wirings` from `extends`.
5. Emit a deterministic `initialization_order` — Kahn's algorithm
   over requires+extends edges with a `BinaryHeap` for stable output;
   an unschedulable graph reports the actual `CyclicGraph` cycle.
6. Produce a per-plugin `target_report` against the requested target,
   and validate `ast_kinds`: a consumed kind that some available
   plugin could produce must have a selected producer
   (`MissingProducer`).

The result is `ResolvedComposition` — selected plugin ids, the
capability→provider map, extension wirings, init order, missing
optionals, target report.  `ResolutionError` is exhaustive and named
per failure mode.  `DefaultHost::resolve_composition` runs the same
check over a *live* registry via `iter_manifests`, so the manifest
world and the registry world meet at one function.

# Kits and configuration {#sec-kits}

## Kits are curated manifests

A `Kit` is the unit of reuse: a `KitManifest` plus the
`available_plugins` the kit crate ships (`kit.rs`).

```rust
pub struct KitManifest {
    pub id: String,
    pub name: String,
    pub plugins: Vec<String>,              // selected plugin ids
    pub target: Option<String>,            // optional target runtime
    pub selectors: Vec<CapabilitySelector>,// provider pins
}
```

`Kit::resolve` filters `available_plugins` to the manifest's selection
and runs the same `resolve` (@sec-compose) with the kit's selectors
and target — curation is manifest-level, so a kit is a *closed* list:
the host does not discover plugins on disk, and a kit requesting an
absent plugin fails loudly.  A kit manifest loads from TOML or JSON
(`KitManifest::load`).  Kits may also be assembled from authored
fragment directories — the language-as-data path published by
`handl-kit-prelude-lang` (`language_from_dir`), where a "kit" is a
directory of YAML `tokens`/`grammar`/`eval`/`types`/`ast`/`caps`/
`options`/`lexer_rules` files merged into a `Language`
[@handl2026kitprelude]; external producers can emit the same schema —
the research stack (`graphopt`) already does [@handl2026graphopt].

## `.handl.toml` and `HostConfig`

`HostConfig` (`config.rs`) is the in-memory shape of `.handl.toml`:
kit references with per-kit `exclude`, direct `plugins`, global
`excludes`, option `overrides`, and `dependencies`/`patch` tables whose
`DependencySpec` (path or git+rev/branch/tag, with `subdir`) resolves
package sources — including the dev-link story where a `[patch]`
entry redirects a committed git source to a sibling checkout.
`HostConfig::from_toml` parses it; the applier crates (`plugin-applier*`)
turn it into registrations and overrides on a `Host`.  Excluding a
kit's plugin does not fork the kit — and it is configuration, not a
security boundary: a loaded plugin shares the process.

## Options are contributions too

`OptionsPlugin` (`options.rs`) is a `RuleAcceptor` whose rule type is
`OptionSchema` — the option system uses the same contribution channel
as every other rule kind:

```rust
pub struct OptionSchema {
    pub id: String,
    pub scope: OptionScope,          // Global | Kit | Node
    pub applies_to: Option<String>,
    pub default: Value,
    pub possible_values: Vec<Value>,
    pub description: String,
}
```

A plugin declares its own tunables with `contribute::<OptionsPlugin>`;
`OptionsPlugin::resolve` merges schema defaults with overrides
delivered through the `option/set` capability into a `ResolvedOptions`
(`get`/`choice`/`is_enabled`), which every operation `Request` carries.
Because options live in the contribution graph, a plugin can introduce
and consume a tunable without touching the host or any other plugin —
the formatter does not know `comment.style` exists; it reads the
resolved value from its request.

## Loading is itself a plugin

The bootstrapping is complete: plugin *loading* is an acceptor with
contributed rules.  `plugin-load` defines `PluginLoader`
(`can_load`/`load` over a `PluginManifest`), a `LoaderRule`
contribution, and a `LoaderHostPlugin` exposing a `load` capability.
`plugin-loader-native`'s `NativeLoader` resolves `manifest.metadata.path`
to a shared library, binds the `handl_plugin_run` C symbol, and wraps it
in a `Plugin` whose `run` serializes the `CapabilityRequest` to JSON,
crosses the boundary, and deserializes the response — with
`check_portable` rejecting non-serializable payload values.  The
extension ABI itself (JSON over a C boundary) is kernel
[@handl2026kernel]; who loads what is platform policy, and here the
policy is: the loader is a plugin that contributes a loader rule to a
loader host.

# Engines as data-driven machinery {#sec-engines}

The `engine-*` layer is the platform's second half: for each stage of
the language pipeline there is an **abstraction crate** — the
operation marker, the request type, the engine trait — and a
**concrete engine** that interprets `Language` data.  All are public
repos in the same family, and all obey the kernel's rule: dispatch on
`Language` data, never a hardcoded kind match.

|| Crate | Contract | Concrete engines |
||---|---|---|
|| `hnl-engine-lex` | `Lexer` marker; `LexerRequest{source, options}`; `LexerEngine::lex(&self, lang, &req) -> Result<Tokens, LangError>` | `hnl-engine-lex-pattern` — tokenizes via `LexerRuleDef` fragments |
|| `hnl-engine-parse` | `Parser` marker; `ParserRequest{tokens, options}`; `ParserEngine::{expression(ctx, rbp), parse(lang, &req)}`; `ParserContext` token cursor | `hnl-engine-parse-pratt` — a Pratt engine over `lang.grammar` |
|| `hnl-engine-transform` | `Transform` marker; `TransformRequest`/`TransformMode`/`TransformOutput`; `TransformEngine::{transform, find_matches}`; `RuleSource`, the `NativeRewrite` seam | rewrite engines interpret `lang.transforms` |
|| `hnl-engine-exec` | `Eval` marker; `EvalRequest{ast, options}`; `EvalEngine::eval(&self, lang, &req) -> Result<Value, LangError>` + `with_modules`/`with_global` wiring | `hnl-engine-exec-tree-walk` — the reference interpreter |

: The staged engine contracts. {#tbl-engines}

`hnl-engine-exec-tree-walk` deserves one sentence: it is the reference
`Model` — it looks up `lang.eval[node.kind]`, obtains the
`EvalSchemeDef`'s `Term`, and walks the term graph directly,
including the arrow-value record form (`{"__arrow__": true, …}`),
the pair/either payload conventions, causal `Loop` semantics, and the
no-scheme fallback that returns `node.payload`.  It carries zero Rust
knowledge of any concrete construct — the same `Term` machinery the
kernel paper describes, interpreted [@handl2026kernel].  The staged
arrow-engine program (staging to explicit process graphs, spatial
execution) is a separate interpretation strategy on the same terms,
kept as a research note [@handl2026sae].

## Binding engines by name

`handl-runtime` (`crates/handl-runtime`) is the composition layer for
engines.  It names no engine crate:

- `EngineRegistry` is five name→engine maps — lex, parse, eval,
  typecheck, compile — populated by the host
  (`register_lex`/`register_parse`/`register_eval`/…).
- `RuntimeConfig` is serializable name-based selection
  (`{lex: "data", parse: "pratt", eval: "tree-walk", typecheck: ""}` —
  empty means unbound), so a kit or config file selects engines *as
  data*; swapping an engine is a config change.
- `Runtime::from_registry` resolves names against the registry and
  exposes staged `lex`/`parse`/`eval`/`compile`/`run_compiled`; an
  unbound stage returns `LangError::NotImplemented`, which makes
  eval-only runtimes (a compiler consuming a pre-parsed `Ast`) a
  natural configuration rather than a special mode.
- `RuntimeFactory`/`RuntimeHandle` let leaf plugins obtain a sub-runtime
  bound to a `Language` without reaching up the dependency graph — the
  factory re-injects itself so modules can recurse.

The eval operation and the eval *engine* are distinct and both real:
`BasicEvaluator` (@sec-operations) composes contributed Rust
`EvalBehavior`s per node kind and owns the yield/exec-control story;
an `EvalEngine` interprets `lang.eval` schemes wholesale.  A host may
bind either — they plug into different seams of the same model.

# host-tensor: a capability surface end to end {#sec-tensor}

`handl-host-tensor` (`handl-lang/host-tensor` [@handl2026hosttensor])
is the public worked example of everything above, in one component.
It provides a dense row-major `f64` tensor behind a `tensor.*`
operation surface — 28 declared ops (creation, numpy-broadcasting
elementwise arithmetic, `matmul`, `conv2d`, pooling, shape ops) plus a
`tensor.derive` registry of hand-maintained adjoints — and it enters a
host without any platform change:

```rust
let module = HandlModule::new("tensor", TENSOR_HNL, &[])
    .with_ops(TENSOR_OPS, Arc::new(tensor_op_registry()));
// registered into the runtime's ModuleRegistry;
// a foreign call to `tensor.matmul` reaches the Rust impl.
```

Three boundary decisions make it a clean example rather than a special
case:

- **The value crosses as data.**  On the `serde_json::Value` boundary
  a tensor is `{"__tensor__": {"shape": [d,…], "data": [x,…],
  "dtype": "f64"}}`.  Engines that know the kernel's
  `TaggedValue::Tensor` decode the tag at the host-call boundary and
  carry it opaquely; engines that do not see a plain object.  No
  engine or language edit was needed to *carry* tensors.
- **Dispatch is the `ModuleLookup` seam.**  The crate ships its
  interface source plus the Rust atoms; a runtime composes it into a
  `HandlModule`, registration places it in the module chain, and
  `call_host("tensor.matmul")` resolves through `ModuleLookup` to the
  `OpFunction` and then the Rust implementation — the same path every
  module uses.
- **Engine choice stays data.**  A `HandlModule` can select its eval
  engine by name through the same `EngineRegistry` (`eval_name`),
  keeping the swap a configuration fact.

The result: a host gains a numeric capability surface — including
registered adjoints an optimisation loop can dispatch by name — by
registering a module, exactly as a host gains `fmt` by registering an
acceptor.

# Design principles {#sec-principles}

The platform's published principles (`docs/site/explanation/
design-principles.md` [@handl2026platformdocs]) are the commitments
this design operationalises:

1. **Everything is a plugin.**  Semantics, tooling, targets, GC, the
   standard library — one trait.  Nothing is privileged except the
   composition vocabulary itself (`Plugin`/`RuleAcceptor`/`Operation`/
   `Behavior`/`Contribution`/`Host`).
2. **The host provides the world.**  No built-ins: which functions
   exist and which effects are permitted is decided by loaded plugins
   (the `ModuleLookup` seam), in the capability sense of
   Miller [@miller2006robust] and the effects-as-capabilities reading
   [@brachthaeuser2020effects] — what the context provides *is* the
   effect surface.
3. **Evaluation is an operation, not a subsystem.**  There is no `VM`
   alongside the operation system; `Vm` is a generic pairing of a
   `CallableLookup` and an environment.
4. **A language is data; engines dispatch on it.**  The `engine-*`
   contracts take `&Language`; a renamed-kind language runs untouched.
5. **Kit-level properties are composition facts.**  Sandboxing is
   "which plugins are loaded"; GC is "which plugin provides it";
   targets are rules.  None is a kernel or platform flag.
6. **Composition over registries.**  One registry, one loading
   algorithm, fixed-point contribution; crate boundaries exist only at
   real dependency seams.

The same ideas recur as engineering choices: `contribute::<P>` is
type-safe delivery with dynamic addressing; deferred contribution
makes order a convenience; manifests make composition *checkable
data*; `RuntimeConfig` makes engine choice *checkable data*; the
loader seam makes even loading *a plugin*.

# Implementation status {#sec-status}

The platform layer is `handl-lang/host`, a cargo workspace; the pieces
this paper describes are:

|| Crate (all under `crates/`) | Contents |
||---|---|
|| `platform` (`handl-platform`) | `Plugin`/`Capability*`/`PluginRegistry`/`DefaultHost`; `Contribution`/`RuleAcceptor`/`Operation`/`Behavior`/`ContributionContext`; the `Format`/`Lint`/`Compile`/`Build`/`Eval` contracts + `Basic*` acceptors; `OptionsPlugin`; `PluginManifest`/`resolve`/`Kit*`/`HostConfig`; `AstNode`; `Boundary`; `Vm` |
|| `plugin-module` | `ModuleRegistry` (`ModuleLookup` impl), `ModuleRuntime` |
|| `plugin-load`, `plugin-loader-native` | `PluginLoader`/`LoaderRule`/`LoaderHostPlugin`; the cdylib `NativeLoader` |
|| `plugin-applier*` | `HostConfig` → host application (`.handl.toml`, CLI, env) |
|| `plugin-ext-*` | published capability *contract surfaces* for the operations layer |
|| `plugin-lib-*` | library plugins — module implementations such as `HandlModule`/`OpFunction` (`plugin-lib-handl`) |
|| `handl-runtime` | `EngineRegistry`, `RuntimeConfig`, `Runtime`, `RuntimeFactory`/`RuntimeHandle` |
|| `handl-kit-*` | kit data assembly — merging `Language` fragments and manifests into loadable kits |

: Host workspace map (public crates; `handl-platform` is the shared
contract). {#tbl-crates}

What is *proven* by the tree: a binary that depends only on
`handl-platform` builds a working tool (`docs/site/tutorials`), the
deferred-contribution and resolution paths are unit-tested in the
crate, and the full pipeline — a `Language` assembled from
`kit-prelude-lang` fragments, interpreted by `engine-*` engines,
extended by `host-tensor` modules — is exercised end to end.

Honest boundaries, stated rather than elided:

- **Contribution order is registration order.**  `load` runs
  `contribute` once per plugin in the order registered (with
  newly-registered plugins visited as the loop grows); it is *not*
  itself the manifest topological order — `resolve` produces that
  order for kits, and deferred rules cover acceptor timing.  A kit
  that wants dependency ordering uses the resolver's
  `initialization_order`.
- **Capability dispatch is last-registration-wins.**  The registry
  index maps a capability to the most recently registered provider;
  the resolver's `provider_map` (selectors, unique provider, highest
  semver, `exclusive` checks) is the *manifest-level* answer, and
  `resolve_composition` surfaces disagreements rather than enforcing
  them during `register`.
- **The boundary is JSON.**  `CapabilityRequest`/`CapabilityResponse`
  and the `AstNode` payload are `serde_json::Value`; non-finite floats
  and non-portable values are boundary concerns the native loader
  checks explicitly (`check_portable`).
- **Not a security model.**  Kit exclusion and `exclusive` resolution
  are correctness tools; plugins share the process.
- **Above the contracts is unpublished.**  The command hosts, the
  release toolchain engines, and the curated kits exist as private
  siblings; the seams they plug into are the public ones described
  here.

# Related work {#sec-related}

**Plugin architectures.**  The contribution model descends from the
extension-point tradition: Gamma and Beck's Eclipse model, where a
plugin declares extension points and contributes extensions to others'
[@gamma2003contributing], and OSGi's service registry with declarative
wiring [@osgi2020core].  The platform's difference is that the
extension *points* are typed (`RuleAcceptor::Rule`) and delivery is
the compiler-checked `contribute::<P>`; Eclipse's loosely-typed
extension registry becomes an associated-type constraint.  Fixed-point
`contribute` is what those systems call declarative assembly done
imperatively — plugins may register plugins mid-load.

**Language workbenches and extensible compilers.**  Spoofax
[@kats2010spoofax], Rascal [@klint2009rascal], JastAdd
[@ekman2007jastadd], Silver [@vanwyk2010silver], and Kiama
[@sloane2011kiama] all attack the language↔tool coupling with
declarative rule systems over syntax; the workbench survey of
Erdweg et al. [@erdweg2013workbenches] is the landscape.  The handl
split is different in kind: those systems make *rules* declarative
inside a fixed workbench, while here the *language* is data and the
*tools* are plugins — the two axes are attacked separately and the
composer between them is this paper.  The independently-extensible
problem is the classical expression problem
[@zenger2005independently]; data-driven AST kinds plus per-operation
behaviors is the platform's answer — a new construct is new rules for
existing operations, and a new operation is a new marker type, neither
touching the other.

**Polyglot hosts and staged interpreters.**  Truffle/Graal is the
polyglot host precedent — one VM hosting many language
implementations [@wuerthinger2013onevm], with partial evaluation
turning interpreter+program into compiled code
[@wuerthinger2017practical].  The kernel cites the Futamura
projection for the same structure [@handl2026kernel]; the platform's
version is coarser and more modular — engines are exchangeable by
name in a registry rather than by partial evaluation of an
interpreter, though the staged-arrow research program aims at the
same territory [@handl2026sae].  Finally-tagless interpretation
[@carette2009finally] is the typed cousin of "one term, many
interpreters" — here the tagless repr is the `Term` IR and the
interpreters are registered engines.  Language servers externalise
tooling behind a protocol [@microsoft2023lsp]; the capability
request is the in-process analogue, with `CapabilityId` playing the
method-name role.  Lua's embeddability — the host owns the runtime,
not vice versa [@ierusalimschy2007lua] — is the deployment stance:
`handl-platform` is a library you compose, not a VM you embed into.

**Within the org.**  The kernel paper owns the calculus and the
`Language` schema [@handl2026kernel]; the research prototype and the
ADR series carry the decision history [@handl2026kernelpoc;
@handl2026adrs]; the platform documentation carries the vetted
explanations this paper condenses [@handl2026platformdocs].  The
theory-as-data / model-as-functor reading (Lawvere
[@lawvere1963functorial]) is the same one the kernel claims: a
`Language` is the theory, an engine is a model, and — one level up —
a `PluginManifest` set is the composition's data and `resolve` its
checker.

# Limitations and open questions

- **Composition is checked, not solved.**  `resolve` is a
  deterministic pass, not a constraint solver: no backtracking version
  negotiation, no dependency *search*.  Version ranges are verified
  (`VersionReq`) but not solved for.  Whether the manifest vocabulary
  needs a real solver is open.
- **Dispatch is linear over rules.**  `Basic*` acceptors scan their
  rule list per node kind; hot paths live in the engines, and a
  kind-indexed dispatch table is a plausible optimisation that has not
  been needed.
- **The two eval paths coexist by design but share no scheduler.**
  `BasicEvaluator` (behavior rules, yield, exec-control) and
  `EvalEngine` (scheme interpretation) answer different needs; a
  unified story — e.g. exec-control hooks inside scheme evaluation —
  is not yet designed.
- **Deferred contribution makes loads order-tolerant, not
  order-independent.**  A `contribute` that *reads* another plugin's
  state still observes registration order; only rule delivery is
  deferred.
- **The contract surface is ahead of the released tools.**  The public
  contracts describe operations whose production engines are private;
  the honesty cost is that `Basic*` acceptors must not be mistaken for
  the canonical pipelines — this paper has tried to keep the two
  roles named distinctly.
